title: Joshua 7:6–15
context: After the defeat at Ai, Joshua and the elders mourn before the ark of the LORD (7:6–9). Joshua’s lament is honest and anxious: he questions why the LORD brought Israel over the Jordan and fears for the LORD’s “great name” among the nations. The LORD answers in 7:10–15 by naming the real cause of the defeat. Israel has transgressed the covenant by taking devoted things, and the LORD will not be with them until the devoted thing is removed. He then sets out a procedure for identifying the guilty party by sacred selection, tribe by tribe, and announces the penalty. The section shows that the problem is not the strength of Ai but a breach of covenant holiness within Israel.

verses.text: Joshua tore his clothes, and fell to the earth on his face before the LORD’s ark until the evening, he and the elders of Israel; and they put dust on their heads.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua tears his clothes, falls “on his face before the LORD’s ark until the evening,” and the elders join him with dust on their heads. These are recognized acts of grief and humiliation. Arminian readers see a fitting response to disaster: leaders take the people’s plight before God rather than simply regrouping, and their humility opens the way for God’s answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joshua instinctively turns to the ark, the sign of God’s covenant presence, recognizing that the defeat must be understood before God. Even before he knows the cause, he treats it as a spiritual matter. Shared ground: both traditions commend the turn to God in public mourning, while noting that the following verses show his prayer still lacks understanding of the real problem.

verses.text: Joshua said, “Alas, Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to cause us to perish? I wish that we had been content and lived beyond the Jordan!
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua’s words, “why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all,” echo Israel’s complaints in the wilderness, wishing they had stayed where they were. Arminian readers note that Scripture records such honest laments without endorsing every word. God permits his servants to pour out confusion and fear, yet the answer in 7:10–11 will correct Joshua’s assumption that the LORD has failed them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Joshua attributes the event directly to God (“why have you brought”), which rightly confesses God’s rule over Israel’s history, even though Joshua misreads his purpose. The problem lies not in God’s faithfulness but in Israel’s sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sincere but mistaken lament, which God answers patiently with truth rather than rejecting the one who prays.

verses.text: Oh, Lord, what shall I say, after Israel has turned their backs before their enemies?
verses.arminianNotes: “Oh, Lord, what shall I say” captures Joshua’s loss for words after Israel “has turned their backs before their enemies.” Arminian readers see here the bewilderment of a faithful leader who does not yet know of the hidden sin. His distress shows how seriously he takes Israel’s calling and how deeply the defeat contradicts what he expected from the LORD’s promises (1:5, 9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joshua’s perplexity arises because he knows God’s promises and cannot reconcile them with what has happened. That tension drives him to God rather than away from him. Shared ground: both traditions see a model of bringing confusion to God in prayer, and both note that the answer will come through God’s word exposing the cause, not through a change in God’s character.

verses.text: For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it, and will surround us, and cut off our name from the earth. What will you do for your great name?”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua fears the Canaanites will “cut off our name from the earth,” and then asks, “What will you do for your great name?” Arminian readers see the prayer rising from concern for Israel’s survival to concern for the LORD’s reputation among the nations. Real prayer engages God’s stated purposes, and Joshua appeals to God’s concern that the nations know him (compare 4:24).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight the appeal to God’s “great name” as the deepest ground of prayer: God acts for the sake of his own glory, and his people’s good is bound up with it. Shared ground: both traditions value this God-centered turn in Joshua’s lament, and both see the answer of verses 10–15 as showing that God’s name is honored by dealing truthfully with sin among his people.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face like that?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers abruptly: “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face like that?” Prayer is not wrong, but at this moment it cannot replace obedience. Arminian readers note that God directs Joshua from lament to action, because the remedy lies in a concrete response to sin that Israel is responsible to carry out.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD’s rebuke is not a rejection of Joshua but a redirection by God’s word. Mourning without knowing the cause cannot heal the breach, so God supplies the diagnosis. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as teaching that prayer and repentance belong together, and that when God reveals sin, the right response is to deal with it rather than remain in general grief.

verses.text: Israel has sinned. Yes, they have even transgressed my covenant which I commanded them. Yes, they have even taken some of the devoted things, and have also stolen, and also deceived. They have even put it among their own stuff.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s charge piles up verbs: Israel has “sinned,” “transgressed my covenant,” “taken some of the devoted things,” “stolen,” “deceived,” and hidden the goods “among their own stuff.” Arminian readers note how one act involves several sins together, and that God treats the deed as a deliberate breach of a known command, for which those who did it are truly accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God says “Israel has sinned,” though one man took the goods. The covenant community is addressed as one, so the guilt rests on the people until the sin is purged. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the theological center of the chapter, showing that covenant breach includes theft from God, deceit, and concealment, and that it affects the whole people.

verses.text: Therefore the children of Israel can’t stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will not be with you any more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel “can’t stand before their enemies” because “they have become devoted for destruction.” Taking what was devoted to the LORD brings the taker under the same status (compare Deuteronomy 7:26, “become a devoted thing like it”). Arminian readers stress the conditional promise: “I will not be with you any more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.” God’s presence is linked to Israel’s response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the seriousness of God’s holiness: what belongs to the LORD cannot be appropriated by his people without bringing them under judgment. The withdrawal of his presence is the gravest consequence, and it is God himself who names the remedy. Shared ground: both traditions read the conditional “unless” as a real call to action, and both see God’s presence, not military power, as Israel’s true strength.

verses.text: Get up! Sanctify the people, and say, ‘Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, for the LORD, the God of Israel, says, “There is a devoted thing among you, Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted thing from among you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua is told to sanctify the people for the next day, as Israel had done before crossing the Jordan (3:5). Arminian readers note that the process gives the whole people a part in preparing to meet God and in removing what defiles the camp. Consecration is a responsive act of the community, preparing to face God’s judgment honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself frames the proceedings with his own word: “There is a devoted thing among you, Israel.” Holiness is defined by God, and the people must come before him on his terms. Shared ground: both traditions see that sin within the covenant people has to be dealt with before God, publicly and seriously, and that consecration is the necessary preparation for judgment and restoration.

verses.text: In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. It shall be that the tribe which the LORD selects shall come near by families. The family which the LORD selects shall come near by households. The household which the LORD selects shall come near man by man.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel is to come near “by your tribes,” then by families, households, and “man by man,” as “the LORD selects.” The method is most likely a sacred lot, though the verse does not specify. Arminian readers note that the process also gives time for the guilty party to come forward, and that Achan does not confess until he is identified (7:19–20).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence directing a process that might seem like chance, in line with Proverbs 16:33: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.” Nothing is hidden from God. Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD himself identifies the guilty, so the outcome is not human guesswork, and that hidden sin cannot remain hidden before him (compare Numbers 32:23).

verses.text: It shall be, that he who is taken with the devoted thing shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the LORD’s covenant, and because he has done a disgraceful thing in Israel.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The guilty one “shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has,” because he has transgressed the LORD’s covenant and “done a disgraceful thing in Israel.” Arminian readers emphasize the stated grounds: the sentence answers a willful breach of a covenant command, given openly in 6:18. The severity reflects how seriously God regarded the sanctity of what was devoted to him in this foundational moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the penalty treats the offender as the devoted thing itself, consistent with 7:12. The language of sacred destruction applies now to one within Israel, showing that herem was about God’s holiness, not ethnicity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly within Israel’s covenant and theocratic setting, and neither treats it as a pattern for the church, which deals with sin through discipline and the gospel.
